newsitem.title: USA: Glickman sees tough resistance to biotech.
newsitem.headline: Glickman sees tough resistance to biotech.

text.p: Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman, rejecting a charge by environmentalists that the U.S. government is too close to big business, urged consumers Friday not to be swayed by "rhetoric and emotion" in a dispute over genetically altered soybeans.
Acknowledging European mistrust of the beans, developed by St. Louis-based Monsanto Co., Glickman reminded consumers that most cancer drugs were based on similar science.

"It is an issue that is very easily whipped up with rhetoric and emotion, and it is incumbent on all leaders to educate people on what the facts are and make sure science is objective," he told reporters at a U.N. food summit in Rome.
"Saying that does not mean we have all the answers or that in a supine or blind way we follow industry," he said in a telephone news conference.
Glickman said the whole area of biotechnology is extremely controversial in Europe, and that public fears are being exploited.

European consumers have been in an uproar the past few weeks over the marketing for the first time of a genetically modified soybean grown in the United States this past season. The soybean is resistant to Monsanto's Roundup pesticide, and a small amount was grown commercially by American farmers this year.

Protesters led by the Greenpeace group have been trying to keep the soybeans out of Europe, and have chained themselves to gates in Germany, occupied the office of the Austrian health minister and climbed to the roof of the headquarters of Swiss food group Nestle SA.
Greenpeace said Friday that U.S. grain giant Cargill took out an injunction banning it from interfering with the arrival this weekend of another load of genetically modified soybeans.

Greenpeace said it faced fines of one million francs ($30,000) an hour if it comes within one kilometre (.6 mile) of the grain ship Stanislaw Kulczynski, which is due to arrive in the Belgian port of Antwerp over the weekend.

Glickman said there is currently "a lot of hostility to science," and that some circles are trying to exploit public fears "about things in the food supply that people don't know about, can't control and think is going to hurt them."

He said this is especially troubling, given the challenges the world faces in feeding a rapidly increasing population -- a population that he said will grow by 2 1/2 billion people in the next 20 years.

"How are we going to feed the world without new technology other than tearing up highly erodible soil, or tearing up the rain forests, or otherwise destroying the environment? There is no way to have it both ways," Glickman said.

Recognising that the opposition to the new soybeans appears to be strongest in Germany, Glickman noted that he met with Germany's minister of agriculture on the issue. He said the German official supports biotechnolgoy, but believes that the modified soybeans should be labelled "under practical circumstances."

Glickman reiterated earlier statements that he is not sure that labeling of gene-modified products such as soybeans can ever be done on a practical basis, but that consumers need to be educated as to the safety and the real benefits of the new products.
